passages.t: The year of release: ‘open your hand’
passages.happening:
“At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts” (verse 1). Every lender is to let go of what a neighbor owes, ‘because the LORD’s time of release has been proclaimed’ (verse 2). A debt owed by a foreigner may still be collected (verse 3).

Moses adds a promise. “There will be no poor among you, however, because the LORD will surely bless you in the land”, if only Israel obeys (verses 4-5).

Then he speaks of what to do when someone is poor. “If there is a poor man among your brothers within any of the gates in the land that the LORD your God is giving you, then you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother. Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs” (verses 7-8).

He names a temptation. A lender might think, ‘The seventh year, the year of release, is near’, and refuse to lend (verse 9). The poor man ‘will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin’. “Give generously to him, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so” (verse 10).

“For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Debt was the main road into poverty in the ancient world. A farmer hit by a bad harvest borrowed seed or food. If he could not repay, he might sell his land, then his children into service, and at last himself.

Kings in Mesopotamia sometimes issued decrees that cancelled certain debts and freed people held for debt. One of the best preserved comes from a king of Babylon in the seventeenth century BC. Such decrees depended on a king's decision. Deuteronomy does something different. It makes release a fixed part of the calendar, owed by law to every Israelite. Mercy is not left to a ruler's mood.

The Hebrew word for the release comes from a verb that means to let drop. Interpreters differ on whether the debts were forgiven entirely or only left uncollected for that year. Jewish tradition took it as full cancellation.

The foreigner of verse 3 is a trader or visitor, not the foreigner who lives among Israel and is protected elsewhere in this book.

Notice how Moses speaks. He does more than give a rule. He speaks to what goes on inside the lender. He names the calculation a careful person would make: the release is near, a loan made now will never come back. He calls that a ‘wicked thought’. The law reaches into the heart and the hand together. The hand is to be open and not shut. The heart is not to be hard, and it is not to be ‘grieved’ in giving.

Verse 9 says that the poor man's cry goes to God, and that God counts the refusal as sin. In this book God is on the side of the one who has nothing.

The word for ‘poor’ or ‘needy’ comes six times in this chapter. It means a person who lacks the basic means of life and can easily be used by others.

Jewish history shows how seriously this law was taken and how hard it was to keep. Jewish tradition tells that around the time of Jesus the teacher Hillel introduced a legal arrangement, called the prosbul, so that people would not refuse to lend as the seventh year came near. That is the very problem verse 9 foresees.
passages.later:
After the exile the people promised to keep this law: “Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow, and will cancel every debt” (Nehemiah 10:31).

Jesus began his work in his home town by reading from Isaiah, in words that draw on these laws of release: ‘to proclaim liberty to the captives’ and ‘the year of the Lord’s favor’ (Luke 4:18-19).

The first church in Jerusalem saw the promise of verse 4 come true among them for a time: “There were no needy ones among them” (Acts 4:34).

John asks the question Moses asks: “If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3:17).
passages.hard:
Verse 4 says, ‘There will be no poor among you’. Verse 11 says there will never cease to be poor. Which is it? And did Jesus mean that poverty cannot be helped?

The two sentences stand a few verses apart, so the writer plainly meant them to stand together.

Most interpreters read verse 4 as a promise with a condition. There need be no poor in Israel if Israel obeys God's laws, and those laws include the release of debts and the open hand (verse 5). Verse 11 speaks of what will happen in a world where people do not fully obey. There will be poor people, and so the command will always apply. Some put it this way: verse 4 is the goal the laws aim at, and verse 11 is the situation they address.

Look closely at how verse 11 runs. It does not say: there will always be poor people, so nothing can be done. It says the opposite: there will always be poor people, ‘that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand’. The lasting presence of the poor is given as the reason for lasting generosity.

When Jesus said, “The poor you will always have with you” (Matthew 26:11), he was quoting this verse to people who knew it. In Mark's account he adds, ‘and you can help them whenever you want’ (Mark 14:7). He was defending a woman who had honored him before his death. He was not excusing anyone from caring for the poor.

So the sentence may never be used as a reason for neglect. A reader who quotes it in order to keep the hand shut is using Moses' words, and Jesus' words, against their own meaning.
passages.asks: Moses knows the reasons a sensible person finds for not giving, and he calls them by name. Ask what calculation you make before you help someone, and whether verse 9 describes it. And ask who near you is poor in the plain sense of this chapter: lacking what life requires. Ask what an open hand toward that person would be.

passages.t: Set free, and not sent away empty
passages.happening:
Moses turns from debts to people. “If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, is sold to you and serves you six years, then in the seventh year you must set him free” (verse 12).

Freedom is not enough. “And when you release him, do not send him away empty-handed. You are to furnish him liberally from your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress” (verses 13-14). The reason: “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (verse 15).

A servant who does not want to leave, ‘because he loves you and your household and is well off with you’, may stay for life, and his ear is pierced at the door as the sign (verses 16-17). The same applies to a female servant.

The master is told not to think the release a hardship. The servant's six years ‘were worth twice the wages of a hired hand’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is the end of the road that began with debt. A person who had lost everything could be sold, or sell himself, into another household to work off what was owed. The law sets a limit of six years.

The same law is in Exodus 21. Deuteronomy adds two things. It says plainly that it covers women as well as men. And it requires that the freed person be sent off with a generous share of animals, grain and wine.

That second addition shows how well the law understands poverty. A person released with nothing has nowhere to go but back into debt. Freedom without the means to live is not yet freedom. So the master must supply a new start, and must do it ‘liberally’. The measure is how much God has given the master.

The reason is Egypt. Israel had itself gone out of slavery loaded with gifts (Exodus 12:35-36). What God did for Israel, the Israelite is to do for the one who served him.

The ceremony of the pierced ear was a public sign, made at the door of the house, that the servant had chosen to belong to that household for good. The law takes it for granted that this would happen only where the servant was loved and well treated.

Verse 18 speaks again to the heart of the one who has to give something up. Moses knows that letting a worker go feels like a loss. He tells the master to count what he has already received.

This law limited servitude. It did not end it. The hard question below faces that.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the first form of this law: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he is to serve you for six years. But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything” (Exodus 21:2).

Jeremiah records a time when Jerusalem kept this law and then broke it. The people freed their servants during a siege and then took them back: ‘you have again forced them to be your slaves’ (Jeremiah 34:16). God called it a profaning of his name.

Leviticus sets a greater release beside this one, every fiftieth year: ‘proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants’ (Leviticus 25:10).
passages.hard:
Why does the law allow a person to be sold into service at all?

That question should be faced honestly, and these notes do not defend slavery.

The law permitted an Israelite to be sold into another's household for debt and to work there without wages. Other laws allowed foreigners to be held for life (Leviticus 25:44-46). That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away.

The law also set limits that its world did not know. The service ended in the seventh year. Women were covered equally. The freed person had to be given the means to live. And all of it was grounded in God's act of freeing Israel from slavery. Many readers see in this a direction set toward freedom. Critics answer that the law still allowed one person to hold another, and that this has to be faced. Both things are true to the text.

The note on Exodus 21 tells the painful history of how such texts were later misused to defend slavery, and why that was wrong.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The site's guide to the slavery texts, and the Reading the Law guide, go further.
passages.asks: The law would not let a person be set free with empty hands. Ask whether the help you give people leaves them able to stand, or only moves them on. And remember what you were given when you had nothing. Ask whether that memory shapes how you treat anyone who works for you or depends on you.

passages.happening:
A short law closes the chapter. “You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks” (verse 19). The firstborn ox is not to be put to work, and the firstborn sheep is not to be shorn.

Each year the family is to eat it before God at the place he chooses (verse 20). An animal with a defect, ‘lame or blind’, is not to be sacrificed. It may be eaten at home like a gazelle or a deer (verses 21-22). Only the blood must not be eaten (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The first male born to a cow, a ewe or a goat belonged to God. The rule goes back to the night of the exodus, when God spared the firstborn of Israel. From then on the first of every womb was his.

The farmer could not use such an animal to make money. He could not put the young ox to the plow or take the wool of the young sheep. It was not his to profit from. Giving the first to God was a way of saying that the whole herd came from him.

Even so, the animal comes back to the family as a meal. Like the tithe in chapter 14, this offering is eaten with joy before God. The pattern is the same throughout these chapters. What is given to God is shared at his table.

An animal with a defect could not be offered. To give God the lame and the blind of the flock, and keep the best, would turn the gift into an insult. But nothing is wasted. The family eats it at home, under the rule about blood from chapter 12.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the origin of the law: “Consecrate to Me every firstborn male. The firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast” (Exodus 13:2).

The prophet Malachi rebuked priests who brought God what they would not give a governor: ‘When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is it not wrong?’ (Malachi 1:8).
passages.asks: Israel gave God the first, and not what was left over. Ask what God gets from you: the first of your time, strength and money, or what remains after everything else has been paid. And notice that what was given came back as a shared meal. Ask whether you think of giving to God as loss.
